name: Venantius Fortunatus
knownFor: Poet from northern Italy who came to Gaul for Martin of Tours, settled at Poitiers beside Radegund's monastery of the Holy Cross, and wrote verse for kings and bishops, Lives of saints, and hymns of the Cross.
dates: No ancient source used here gives any year of his life. Born about 530 and died about 600 in W. D. Foulke's note to Paul the Deacon; M. A. Luchi reports the belief that he was born about 530, and puts his death early in the seventh century; Hugh Williams says he died about 609. Bruno Krusch puts his coming to Gaul in 565; Friedrich Leo's index places it between 561 and 567
place: Born near Ceneda and Treviso in northern Italy; trained at Ravenna; Poitiers
role: Poet; priest, and bishop of Poitiers in Paul the Deacon's account

keyWorks.title: Life of Saint Martin
keyWorks.about: the life of Martin of Tours in four books of verse, as Gregory of Tours and Paul the Deacon both say; its fourth book names his birthplace and the healing of his eyes

keyWorks.title: Poems
keyWorks.about: verse for kings, bishops and friends, poems to Radegund and Agnes, and the hymns of the Cross, among them Pange lingua and Vexilla Regis prodeunt, given here in Latin only

keyWorks.title: Lives of saints in prose
keyWorks.about: among them Hilary of Poitiers, Germanus of Paris, Marcellus of Paris and Radegund; Paul the Deacon says he wrote the deeds of many saints, part in prose and part in verse

traces: His Life of Radegund is the first book of her Life; Baudonivia, a nun of Holy Cross, wrote the second to tell what he passed over.
O. M. Dalton says the arrival of the relic of the Cross at Radegund's monastery was celebrated by Fortunatus in several hymns, the most famous beginning Vexilla Regis prodeunt.
remembered: Paul the Deacon calls him second to none of the poets in soft and fluent speech, and wrote his epitaph at Poitiers at the request of the abbot Aper.
Gregory of Tours calls him his venerable fellow servant, and in his book on Martin's miracles wishes that Fortunatus were there to write them.
An epitaph printed in Alcuin's works in Migne calls him an ornament of the Church who wrote many songs of the saints in verse.

uncertain: Whether and when he was bishop. Paul the Deacon says he was ordained at Poitiers, first priest and then bishop, and Baudonivia calls him bishop. Gregory of Tours calls him a priest each time he names him. O. M. Dalton, Gregory's English translator, thinks he was consecrated only after Gregory's death, citing his own Introduction, which is not among the sources used here; M. A. Luchi gives the same reason and says the year is hard to fix. No source used here dates the bishopric. An unsigned note in Migne answers earlier scholars who struck him from the list of the bishops of Poitiers.

His years. No ancient source used here gives any year of his birth, his coming to Gaul or his death. The years on this card are W. D. Foulke's, M. A. Luchi's, Hugh Williams's, Bruno Krusch's and Friedrich Leo's. Paul the Deacon says only that he left Italy a little before the Lombards invaded it.

The healing of his eyes at Ravenna is told three ways. Paul the Deacon puts it at the church of Saint Paul and Saint John, at a lamp in a window by an altar of Martin. Gregory of Tours, who had it from Fortunatus, puts the lamp beneath a painted image of Martin. Fortunatus's own poem says Martin gave the light back to Felix of Treviso and to him. W. D. Foulke, citing R. Jacobi's study of Paul's sources, says Paul took the story from Fortunatus's poem.

His hymns. No English translation of them is among the sources used here; the Latin is in Friedrich Leo's edition and, under his name, in Migne's volume of Alcuin. The count of 600 hymns is W. D. Foulke's, with no source used here behind it.

Some Lives under his name. Bruno Krusch denies him the Life of Medard, and says the Life of Remigius is wrongly given to him; others gave the Life of Marcellus to another Fortunatus, which Krusch rejects.
Fortunatus of Grado, Fortunatus of Naples and Fortunatus of Fano are other men.
